parsed.same_study_reason: Both lists concern estimates of macroeconomic damages from temperature shocks, their dynamic persistence, extrapolation to sustained warming, and translation into social-cost-of-carbon or welfare calculations.

pairs.reason: Both address specification of the temperature time-series/shock process. A1 worries that too few lags miss longer historical cycles, whereas B1 worries that forecast-error horizon and lag choices build persistence assumptions into the shocks and implied damages.

Both concern interpretation of the damage associated with a 1°C temperature change. A1 focuses on linear scaling from much smaller shocks, while B4 focuses on post-shock persistence and its translation into the damage kernel.

Both question functional-form assumptions used to turn temperature responses into long-run damage or welfare conclusions. A1 concerns level versus nonlinear or permanent-growth effects in the empirical temperature model; B5 concerns the structural welfare model, TFP-only damages, and its damage-kernel restriction.

Both identify weak support for linearly extrapolating small historical temperature shocks to larger warming. B9 is broader because it extends the concern to multi-degree warming, tails, tipping points, and adaptation regimes.

Both question whether the reported confidence regions have valid finite-sample inference in a complicated time-series/local-projection setting. A2 states the problem broadly and asks for simulations, while B2 specifies overlapping long-horizon outcomes, persistent regressors, and specification sensitivity.

Both discuss the adequacy of the reported uncertainty intervals. A2 concerns their frequentist coverage under few observations and many parameters; B6 concerns omitted structural, climate-response, extrapolation, and measurement uncertainties.

Both concern whether short-horizon estimates support a long-run, permanent-warming damage and SCC mapping. A3 is broader in seeking longer-run effects and SCC sensitivity, whereas B4 identifies persistence estimation and the damage-kernel translation as the specific channel.

Both question extrapolating observed dynamic effects beyond the reported horizon when constructing welfare or SCC results. B5 is broader because it also challenges the representative-agent model, TFP-only damage channel, and other structural omissions.

Both concern long-run damage and SCC conclusions beyond the observed 10-year horizon. A3 asks whether those effects and SCC values are robust; B6 says the displayed uncertainty bands fail to incorporate long-horizon extrapolation uncertainty.

Both concern translating short-run historical shock estimates into damages from sustained warming. A3 focuses on an insufficient outcome horizon and long-run SCC sensitivity, while B9 focuses on nonlinear extrapolation from small shocks to large warming.

Both question the reliability of inference for the long-horizon time-series estimates. A5 identifies too few observations relative to parameters and doubtful asymptotic confidence intervals; B2 identifies overlapping outcomes, persistent regressors, and specification choices as sources of biased standard errors.

Both address what the reported confidence intervals establish for the reduced-form estimates. A5 challenges their finite-sample/asymptotic validity, whereas B6 says they omit deeper non-estimation uncertainty.

Both refer to the small annual-observation global temperature–GDP design. A5 argues that small N relative to parameters undermines asymptotic interval approximations; B11 argues that small N prevents conclusive exclusion of unobserved global confounders.

Both invoke the limited sample as a reason for caution. A6 gives only a general request for more data and robustness checks, while B11 identifies a specific identification consequence: inability to rule out global confounding.
